newsitem.title: UK: IGC expert raises fear over quality of world wheat.
newsitem.headline: IGC expert raises fear over quality of world wheat.

text.p: The quality of world wheat crops is one of the main problems facing the grain industry this year, an International Grains Council official said on Wednesday.
IGC assistant executive director Bill De Maria told BBC radio most regions had been affected by problems of some kind even though the quantity of global harvests was rising.

"Overall I think a problem this year will be one of quality in most of the major producing regions of the world, even with the U.S. winter wheat, which accounts for very large proportion of total wheat trade," De Maria said in an interview on the "Farming Today" programme.
"Average (U.S. winter wheat) protein levels are in single (percentage) figures in many areas, which is unusually low."
Protein is a key ingredient of wheat used to mill flour.
De Maria noted that U.S. spring wheat, which is now being harvested, had seen wheat scab reported in some regions.
IGC estimates published last week point to a higher world wheat harvest of 585 million tonnes, compared with a previous monthly estimate of 579 million and last year's 582 million.
However, grain traders expect a larger-than-usual proportion of this wheat to be suitable only for animal feed, adding to ample supply of other feed grains and competing substitutes.
The European Union this year is heading for a second near-record wheat crop in a row but much of it will be below flour milling quality because of drought then rain, analysts say.
Quality is also worrying many farmers in eastern Europe after rain and last month's heavy flooding.
De Maria said he was reluctant, however, to predict major volume losses, since eastern Europe had also recovered from a disastrous drought the previous year.
"The only countries that have reported sizeable decreases in the expected outturns are Poland and (the former) Czechoslovakia," he said.

De Maria said it was too early too guess the full impact of the El Nino dry weather pattern which has created worries about Australia's grain harvest. But with Australian wheat output already seen falling to 16 million tonnes from last year's record 23.5 million, El Nino could push up world prices.
De Maria said the initiative was mostly with importers who had been "holding back a little" in the hope that prices would fall from current levels near $140 per tonne.
"I do feel however that this might be somewhat short-lived and subject to turnaround if we do see the impact of El Nino being more severe than expected," he said.
